# The same servers on local Kubernetes

The lab's Postgres images also run as pods on a local Kubernetes cluster. That makes it possible to
run the pgvector notebook's concurrency tests against a pod and compare them with the compose
results. Every local cluster here is a container inside Docker Desktop's VM, on the same cores as
compose. So the comparison measures what Kubernetes networking and pods add, not a faster or
slower machine.

## kind, k3d and k3s

The lab supports three ways to get a cluster. kind runs stock Kubernetes in a container, k3d runs
k3s (a trimmed Kubernetes distribution) through its own command-line tool, and k3s can also run in
a single container started from Python. Each one exposes the two Postgres pods on its own pair of
ports:

```bash
just k8s-up kind     # stock Kubernetes, ports 5434 / 5435
just k8s-up k3d      # k3s through k3d, ports 5436 / 5437
just k8s-up k3s      # k3s in one container from Python, ports 5438 / 5439
just k8s-test kind   # the pgvector notebook against the cluster
```

| | kind | k3d |
|---|---|---|
| distribution | stock Kubernetes, built with kubeadm | k3s: one binary, SQLite datastore, trimmed components |
| node image | `kindest/node`, 1.3 GB | `rancher/k3s`, about 250 MB |
| cluster create | about 60 s with the image local | about 15 s after the first pull |
| host ports | mapped straight onto the node container | on a separate load-balancer container |
| loading a local image | `kind load docker-image` | `k3d image import` |
| extras by default | none | Traefik ingress and a local-path storage class |

For the benchmark, the choice of cluster does not change the result. Pick kind when you want stock
Kubernetes, and k3d when you want a cluster that is small and fast to create.

## k3s from Python, with no cluster tool at all

The third option needs nothing but Docker. Docker Desktop's own Kubernetes can only be switched on
in its settings, and kind's node needs kubeadm to run inside it, so neither can be started from the
Docker SDK (docker-py). k3s can, because it is one binary that bootstraps the whole cluster by
itself. That is also why k3d is only a thin wrapper around the Docker client.

`k8s/k3s.py` does the same job as k3d in about 150 lines of docker-py:

1. It runs `rancher/k3s` as a privileged container and waits for the node.
2. It streams images in from the local Docker cache (`docker save` into `ctr images import`), so
   nothing is pulled twice.
3. It drops the manifests into k3s's auto-deploy directory, which k3s applies on its own, so no
   `kubectl` call is needed.
4. It waits for the pods, and for Postgres to answer on the host port.

A cold start takes about 40 seconds, and about 10 when the container already exists. The pgvector
notebook calls the script itself when it is pointed at `k3s-pg16`. So the Kubernetes run works on a
clean machine that has only Docker installed.
